title: 3-Read Friday #114
author: Craig Barton
summary: Issue 114 of Craig Barton's 3-Read Friday curates three posts on prior knowledge, procedural fluency, and graphing, drawing added depth from the linked source pieces. Efrat Furst's essay argues that the maxim 'learning depends most on what learners already know' needs a sharper qualifier: an extensive meta-analysis by Simonsmeier found prior knowledge strongly predicts future knowledge but not knowledge gain — the 'prior knowledge paradox' — because whether prior knowledge helps depends on mediating factors like whether it is active, relevant, and congruent. Bill McCallum rebuilds the definition of procedural fluency from the ground up, arguing it has been muddied by loose talk of flexibility and automaticity. Dylan Kane's 'Slow Reveal Graphs Are Awesome' describes a daily routine, borrowed from Jenna Laib, in which students see a graph revealed in stages; Kane reports that a student who had only seen conventional bar graphs described a valid but unconventional graph as 'facing the wrong way,' illustrating how narrow graphical exposure narrows what students believe is possible. All three pieces share a structural theme: standard practice has been under-specified, and the fix is sharpening the definition or the exposure, not adding more of the same.
points: Furst's key insight refines the prior knowledge maxim using Brod's and Simonsmeier's research: it is the structure of prior knowledge (active, relevant, congruent) that determines whether new learning connects to it, not simply whether relevant knowledge exists in memory.

The 'prior knowledge paradox' — strong prior knowledge predicts future knowledge but not knowledge gain — means teachers cannot assume more background knowledge automatically produces more learning; the mediating factors matter more than the raw amount.

McCallum's procedural fluency critique targets loose terminology: defining fluency around its functional purpose rather than surface features (flexibility, automaticity) produces a tighter, more useful classroom standard.

Kane's slow reveal graphs routine exposes a graphical poverty in school mathematics: when students see only conventional formats, any valid alternative registers as an error rather than another legitimate way to represent the same data.

All three articles converge on the same corrective move: standard educational practice is often under-specified, and sharpening the definition — of prior knowledge's role, of fluency, of what a graph can look like — does more work than adding more content.
quotes: Furst argues that the famous maxim — learning depends most on what the learner already knows — needs a sharper edit: it's not just what learners know, but how that knowledge is structured. Whether it's shallow or deep, she suggests, should be the first thing teachers weigh — and it flips everything that follows.

An enlightening meta-analysis by Simonsmeier (2022) explores in depth the relation between prior knowledge and learning. They arrive at a complex and somewhat surprising conclusion: while prior knowledge strongly predicts future knowledge, it does not necessarily predict knowledge gain (which measures learning).

Brod (2021), in his comment on this meta-analysis, suggests a more concise way forward by highlighting the underlying mechanisms by which prior knowledge affects learning. Brod identifies three main sequentially dependent factors and suggests that to know whether prior knowledge helps or hinders learning, we must ask whether it is active, relevant, and congruent.

McCallum argues that procedural fluency has been muddied by loose talk of "flexibility" and "automaticity," so he rebuilds the term from the ground up. The result is a tighter, more functional definition — one centred on what fluency is actually for.

Kane argues that school maths shows pupils such a narrow slice of what graphs can look like that one of his students thought a perfectly normal graph was “facing the wrong way.” His fix is a simple daily routine, via a cracking website, and a quiet case for letting kids learn surprising things about the world.
I asked my students what they noticed. They made a few observations. One student said, "it's facing the wrong way.
In school math, we tend to only show students a very small slice of what graphs can look like. That's partly for practical reasons, to keep things simple and manageable.
